report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Investigation summary

What happened

On 18/06/2026 a Saltbush Air 50-seat twin-turboprop, registered VH-SBQ, rejected its take-off on runway 09 at Tarlton Springs Aerodrome as SB512 and overran the runway end. All times are local time (UTC+10). The roll began at 17:30, five minutes after the end of civil twilight, with 44 passengers, 2 flight crew and 1 cabin crew on board. The first officer called two kangaroos crossing the runway, and the pilot in command rejected the take-off at 118 kt, 6 kt above the V1 of 112 kt. The aircraft struck both animals about one second after the reject began. It left the sealed surface at about 21 kt at 17:30:51 and stopped at 17:30:57, upright, 62 m into the 90 m runway end safety area.

The aircraft sustained substantial damage, and two kangaroos were killed. There were nil serious injuries, and one cabin crew member reported bruising during the disembarkation. The aerodrome was closed for 4 hours 20 minutes.

What the investigation found

The crew's response limited the outcome. Maximum braking was established 2 seconds after the decision, against a fleet mean of 3.2 seconds, and the aircraft stopped with no fire.

The animals reached the runway through a northern boundary fence recorded as failed in 04/2023 and deferred unfunded at three budget rounds. It is likely that the unrepaired fence contributed to this, although it was not shown that a replacement would have excluded kangaroos. The aerodrome held no documented wildlife plan because the AS-139 threshold did not apply to it, and on balance that left the fence without an owner as a wildlife control. Departure fell in the period in which 38 of the 41 logged kangaroo entries were timed, which likely contributed to the animals being present.

The operator's runway inspection requirement could not apply at Tarlton Springs because Appendix 8A admitted an aerodrome only after a reported company strike, and that very likely left the requirement unarmed. No inspection was requested, which likely contributed to the animals being on the runway. The evening service had been approved without reopening the daylight-only route risk assessment, so the roll took place in darkness, and darkness probably contributed to the late sighting.

The reject above V1 extremely likely contributed to the overrun. No training or guidance covered an obstruction on the runway during the roll, and it is likely that this contributed to the reject above V1. A reconstruction indicated that rejecting was probably the safest course available, although this did not make the decision compliant with Part B 4.6.4. The strike left deceleration about 15% below the certified value, and the late reject and the strike together carried the aircraft past the end.

Two further matters increased risk without influencing this occurrence: the evening rotation roster and the monitoring of floor escape path lighting, which is still being examined. Whether four northern edge lights above nominal intensity delayed detection, and whether the crew were fatigued, could not be determined, because the evidence on each was evenly balanced.

What has been done as a result

The aerodrome operator funded the fence replacement for 09/2026 and installed a temporary electric wire on 25/06/2026. The operator amended Appendix 8A by TR-2026-04 on 26/06/2026 to list Tarlton Springs, and suspended the evening service. Two recommendations to the operator remain open. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the regulator's name and any notification requirements.]

Safety message

A control that can be triggered only by the outcome it exists to prevent gives no protection before that outcome. Operators should list aerodromes on wildlife exposure, not reported strikes, and give crews guidance and practice for an obstruction on the runway at and after V1.

The occurrence

Before the departure

The aerodrome operator carried out the day's only runway inspection at 07:35, before the first scheduled arrival, and recorded the result as "movement area clear". No further inspection was carried out or requested that day.

SB512 was the fifth sector of the crew's duty. The crew had signed on at 06:30 for three sectors (Port Carrick to Hensby, Hensby to Mardle Creek and Mardle Creek to Port Carrick). The evening rotation (SB511 Port Carrick to Tarlton Springs and SB512 Tarlton Springs to Port Carrick) was added that morning when a member of the rostered crew reported unfit. The aircraft was a 50-seat twin-turboprop, registered VH-SBQ, with 44 passengers, 2 flight crew and 1 cabin crew on board. The doors were closed at 17:16, and SB512 was scheduled off blocks at 17:20.

Tarlton Springs has no control tower, so the crew made their own broadcasts on the common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF). At 17:21:50 the crew keyed the pilot-activated runway lighting, and the pilot in command said that this gave 30 minutes on the timer. At 17:29:10 the crew broadcast that they were lining up on runway 09 for departure to Port Carrick. The crew did not request a runway inspection, the aerodrome did not offer one, and no wildlife transmission appears on the CTAF in the preceding 90 minutes. The aerodrome was in darkness. Sunset was at 16:58, civil twilight ended at 17:25, and moonrise was not until 22:41. The wind from the aerodrome weather information service was 090 at 6 kt.

The take-off roll and the reject

The first officer was pilot flying. Power was set at 17:30:02 with both engines at 98.4% and 98.5% torque, and the 80 kt cross-check at 17:30:15 was normal with no caution or warning active. The pilot in command called V1, calculated at 112 kt for 20,800 kg, flap 10 and a 5 kt headwind component, at 17:30:29.

At 17:30:31 the first officer called "Roos - roos, roos, on the left, they're on the -". The first officer saw two kangaroos crossing the runway from the northern side to the south, at an estimated range of around 200 m. The aircraft reached VR, 116 kt, in the same second, and no rotate call was made. At 17:30:32 the pilot in command said "Stopping. I have control." Both power levers reached flight idle within 0.6 seconds, at 118 kt. This was 6 kt and 3 seconds past V1, at 1,152 m along the runway, with 695 m of sealed surface remaining (Figure 3).

The pilot in command's air safety report states that, after the first officer's call, they looked up and saw two large animals already on the sealed surface, moving across the centreline. On the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) after the stop, however, the pilot in command said to the first officer "I never had them. I was heads-in on the engine page after V one." The two accounts differ, and the first officer said on the CVR that the animals "came out of the dark on the left of the strip".

The aircraft struck both animals at 17:30:33 at 114 kt, one second after the reject began, with torque already down to 12% and 9%. The flight data recorder (FDR) recorded a lateral acceleration spike of 0.31 g right and a vertical spike of 1.48 g. The first officer said on the CVR that they "took one on the prop". Maximum braking was established at 17:30:34, 2 seconds after the decision. At 17:30:36 reverse was selected on the No. 1 engine only, and the pilot in command said that number two was not coming. The No. 2 propeller RPM decayed from the moment of impact and the No. 2 reverse interlock did not make.

At 17:30:47 the pilot in command said "We're not stopping on it". The aircraft left the sealed surface at the end of runway 09 at 17:30:51 at 21 kt, and deceleration fell from 2.6 m/s2 on the seal to 1.9 m/s2 in graded gravel. It came to rest at 17:30:57, 62 m into the 90 m runway end safety area (RESA) and 28 m short of the end of the prepared safety area, upright, on the extended centreline, with the nose wheel in graded gravel. There was no fire.

After the stop

The pilot in command set the parking brake and shut both engines down, which the FDR records at 17:31:26. The pilot in command saw no fire indications and no abnormal indications, and did not order an evacuation. The cabin was told to remain seated. At 17:31:54 the pilot in command reported on the CTAF that the aircraft had gone off the end of runway 09 and was stopped in the gravel with 44 passengers and three crew, no injuries reported and no fire, and asked for the aerodrome emergency plan to be activated and a vehicle sent. The aerodrome reporting officer activated the plan at 17:32:10, dispatched a vehicle, and broadcast that the runway was obstructed and the aerodrome closed. Asked about injuries, the pilot in command replied that no assistance was required at that stage.

The pilot in command told the cabin that they would disembark by the forward door onto the ground, "nice and slow, no rush, no evacuation". The CVR recorded the forward airstair operating at 17:34:40. No evacuation was commanded and no slides were deployed, and the main cabin lights were on throughout. The notification and the operator's records give 4 minutes 8 seconds as the time until passengers were clear, but the airstair operated 3 minutes 43 seconds after the stop at 17:30:57, and the timeline entry for the disembarkation runs to 17:38:48. [NOT ESTABLISHED: what the 4 minutes 8 seconds is measured from.] Drug and alcohol tests on both flight crew were negative.

Damage, injuries and the runway survey

The No. 2 propeller had three blades damaged beyond repairable limits, one blade tip separated, and animal tissue in two blade roots, and the engine required a shock-load inspection. The right inboard flap was crushed over 0.9 m of span and the wing lower surface was holed aft of the No. 2 nacelle. The right main gear doors were distorted, and the lower right fuselage skin was punctured. Both right main tyres deflated through the fuse plugs, and brake energy reached 84% of the certified maximum, with no brake fire. There were nil serious injuries, and one cabin crew member later reported bruising during the disembarkation. Two kangaroos were killed.

The runway survey recovered two carcasses at 1,188 m and 1,221 m from the runway 09 threshold. It found continuous tyre marks from 1,160 m to the runway end and a nose wheel rut continuing to a stopping point 62 m into the RESA, on the extended centreline (Figure 3). The aerodrome was closed for 4 hours 20 minutes. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the time the aerodrome reopened.]

Context

This section gives the background needed to follow the analysis.

Aircraft and operator

Saltbush Air operated SB512 with VH-SBQ, a 50-seat twin-turboprop. The crew planned the take-off at 20,800 kg with flap 10 and a V1 of 112 kt, using a 5 kt headwind component in the performance entry. The scheduled accelerate-stop distance required was 1,780 m against an ASDA of 1,847 m, a margin of 67 m. [NOT ESTABLISHED: aircraft type designation and manufacturer, aircraft age, and maintenance status before the occurrence.]

Flight crew

The pilot in command held 8,410 hours total, including 2,140 on type, and had been in command for 3 years 1 month. Their last cyclic simulator session was on 11/03/2026 and their last line check on 02/12/2025, both satisfactory. They had no prior occurrence history.

The first officer held 1,655 hours total, including 405 on type, and had been with the company for 14 months. Their last cyclic simulator session was on 28/04/2026, with all items satisfactory. They had flown two previous sectors into Tarlton Springs, both in daylight, on 09/01/2026 and 17/02/2026.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: licence and medical details for the flight crew, and cabin crew details.]

Duty

The crew signed on at 06:30 for a duty of five sectors. The take-off was 11 hours 00 minutes into a duty planned at 13 hours 00 minutes, against a maximum of 13 hours 30 minutes for five sectors with this sign-on. The pilot in command's duty and rest in the 7 days before the occurrence were within the company's limits, with no variations applied.

The first three sectors were Port Carrick to Hensby, Hensby to Mardle Creek and Mardle Creek to Port Carrick. The evening rotation (SB511 Port Carrick to Tarlton Springs and SB512 Tarlton Springs to Port Carrick) was added on the morning of 18/06/2026 when a member of the rostered crew reported unfit. A ground delay in Port Carrick during the third sector was recovered on the Tarlton Springs turnaround, and SB512 departed on schedule.

The evening rotation operated on 289 days from 14/07/2025 to 18/06/2026. On each of those days it was rostered as the fourth and fifth sectors of a Port Carrick-based duty signing on between 06:00 and 07:00, planned at between 12 hours 45 minutes and 13 hours 15 minutes. On six of those days a member of the rostered crew reported unfit and a crew already on duty took over the rotation, which extended that crew's day from three sectors to five. 18/06/2026 was the sixth.

Aerodrome

Tarlton Springs is a certified aerodrome with no control tower, so crews made their own broadcasts on the CTAF. It has a single runway, 09/27. The runway edge lighting is pilot-activated, runs for 30 minutes at one fixed setting that crews cannot vary, and was found set at stage 3. Route risk assessment RRA-041 records a single runway with no lighting redundancy, no alternate within 200 nm at night and limited engineering support.

The ASDA for runway 09 was 1,847 m and the RESA was 90 m. Aerodrome elevation was 412 ft. A telecommunications mast stood 3,400 m beyond the end of runway 09 and 260 m north of the extended centreline, with its top 184 ft above aerodrome elevation. The heaviest scheduled aeroplane was the 22,900 kg twin-turboprop used on the Saltbush Air service, and the aerodrome handled 61,400 passenger movements in 2025. [NOT ESTABLISHED: runway length, width and surface specification, and TORA and TODA.]

Weather and light

The automatic observations at 16:00, 16:30, 17:00 and 18:00 gave wind 080 to 090 at 6 to 8 kt, visibility 9999 and no rain. The AWIS heard by the crew before line-up was 090 at 6 kt.

Sunset was at 16:58 and civil twilight ended at 17:25. Moonrise was not until 22:41, with the moon a waning crescent 14% illuminated. The roll began at 17:30, 5 minutes after the end of civil twilight, so no natural ambient light fell on the strip.

Wildlife at the aerodrome

The aerodrome's wildlife sighting log for 01/01/2025 to 18/06/2026 holds 46 entries. Forty-one record kangaroos on or adjacent to the movement area, 38 of those 41 are timed between one hour before and two hours after last light, and eleven record animals on the sealed surface of runway 09/27. The log is a paper register held in the aerodrome office. It is not reported to any operator, and the aerodrome reporting officer confirmed that no airline had asked for it.

The aerodrome held one runway inspection on 18/06/2026, at 07:35 before the first arrival. Aerodrome Manual 6.3 provides for further inspections on the request of the reporting officer or a pilot in command.

External requirement

Aerodrome Standard AS-139 section 10.4 sets the wildlife requirements for certified aerodromes:

  • "10.4.1 The operator of a certified aerodrome must take reasonable measures to reduce the risk to aircraft operations presented by wildlife on or in the vicinity of the aerodrome."
  • "10.4.2 The operator of a certified aerodrome must prepare, implement and maintain a documented wildlife hazard management plan where the aerodrome is used by aeroplanes having a maximum take-off weight exceeding 27,000 kg, or serves more than 350,000 passenger movements in a calendar year."
  • "10.4.3 Where subsection 10.4.2 does not apply, the measures taken under 10.4.1 need not be documented, but the aerodrome operator must be able to demonstrate what measures are in place."

Tarlton Springs was below both limbs of 10.4.2, so it held no wildlife hazard management plan and was not in breach of the standard.

Operator procedures and performance data

Part A 8.14.2 of the Saltbush Air Operations Manual requires a runway inspection before the first departure after last light at aerodromes listed in Appendix 8A:

  • "At an aerodrome listed in Appendix 8A, the pilot in command shall request a runway inspection from the aerodrome operator prior to the first departure after last light, and shall not commence the take-off roll until the result of that inspection has been passed."

Part A 8.14.3 requires no specific action at other aerodromes. Appendix 8A lists an aerodrome where a wildlife strike involving a company aircraft has been reported there within the preceding 24 months (Figure 1). It listed nine aerodromes on 18/06/2026. Tarlton Springs was not among them and had never been listed. The list was last reviewed on 03/03/2025.

Part B 4.6.4 states: "At or above V1 the take-off shall be continued." (Figure 4). Part B appendix 4C takes the take-off data from the Aeroplane Flight Manual and assumes failure of the critical engine at V1, automatic feathering of that propeller, an otherwise undamaged aeroplane in the take-off configuration, and the operating engine at take-off power. The appendix sets a minimum gross climb gradient of 2.4% with one engine inoperative.

The recurrent training syllabus TRG-SYL-07, module 4, has four scripted simulator scenarios: engine failure at 90 kt, engine fire at 100 kt, configuration warning at 85 kt, and engine failure at V1 plus 5 kt, continued. All are aircraft system events. In the 2025 to 2026 cycle 214 crew completed the module, and no crew had been presented with an external obstruction scenario in the five cycles held on file.

Organisational history

RRA-041 issue 3 (11/2022) is the current route risk assessment for Tarlton Springs. It carries the operating restriction "daylight operations only pending review of night lighting and diversion fuel policy". Change management record CMR-2025-118, approved by the Head of Flying Operations on 22/05/2025, added an evening rotation from 14/07/2025. It assessed the change as "schedule change only" and recorded "Route risk assessment review required: No." No issue 4 of RRA-041 exists.

The aerodrome's works register item WR-221, raised in 04/2023, recorded four displaced panels and strained wire on the northern boundary between the 700 m and 1,300 m runway markers, with animals observed passing through, and estimated replacement at $41,000. It was deferred at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 budget rounds, each time with the entry "defer, unfunded, review next cycle". Item WR-263, raised in 02/2026, recorded the same section as "deteriorating further". A site inspection on 23/06/2026 found a continuous 140 m section with the bottom two wires separated from the posts and a clear animal pad through the fence at the 1,050 m mark (Figure 2).

[NOT ESTABLISHED: who owns the aerodrome beyond the council works register, and the regulator's oversight arrangements.]

Safety analysis

Introduction

This analysis follows the sequence of conditions that put two kangaroos on the runway at Tarlton Springs, the controls that did not find or show them to the crew, the decision made when they were seen, and the stop that followed. It begins with the crew's braking, which limited the outcome. It then takes the route of the animals to the runway, the reasons they were neither found nor seen before the take-off roll, and the way the reject decision and the strike combined to carry the aircraft past the end of the sealed surface. Two matters that could not be settled are discussed separately, followed by two factors that increased risk without influencing this occurrence and the hypotheses that were considered and not found to contribute.

What limited the outcome

The stop was begun quickly and well executed, and it reduced the severity of the overrun. The power levers reached flight idle 0.6 seconds after the decision, and maximum braking was established at 17:30:34, 2 seconds after it, against a fleet mean of 3.2 seconds. Anti-skid was active on all four wheels and brake energy reached 84% of the certified maximum without a brake fire. Reverse was selected on No. 1 within 4 seconds. The aircraft left the sealed surface at about 21 kt and stopped 62 m into the 90 m runway end safety area, upright and on the extended centreline. A stop begun at the fleet mean response would have carried the aircraft an estimated further 30 to 40 m, close to the far edge of the safety area, so the quick response very likely decreased the risk of the outcome.

Why animals reached the runway

The northern perimeter fence was the route by which the animals reached the movement area. The aerodrome operator's works register recorded in 04/2023 that four panels were displaced and wire strained between the 700 m and 1,300 m markers, with animals observed passing through. Replacement was estimated at $41,000. The item was deferred unfunded at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 budget rounds, each time for review in the next cycle, and a later item in 02/2026 recorded the section as deteriorating further. The site inspection on 23/06/2026 found a continuous 140 m section with the bottom two wires separated from the posts and a clear animal pad through it at the 1,050 m mark (Figure 2). That pad was 138 m before the first carcass and on the same side of the runway, and the carcasses lay at 1,188 m and 1,221 m (Figure 3).

The register did not state a replacement specification, and kangaroos can clear a stock fence, so an intact fence might not have stopped these animals. The sighting log also does not show where any of its 41 kangaroos came onto the aerodrome. However, the pad shows the route these two animals used, and the register had recorded animals passing through that section since the day the item was raised. A fence repaired in 2023 would have closed that route in 06/2026. The weakness in the argument is the unknown effectiveness of the replacement, so it is likely that the unrepaired fence contributed to the animals reaching the runway.

The fence was a deferrable works item partly because the standard did not require anything more. AS-139 10.4.2 requires a documented wildlife hazard management plan only where an aerodrome is used by aeroplanes above 27,000 kg maximum take-off weight or serves more than 350,000 passenger movements a year. Tarlton Springs' heaviest scheduled aeroplane is 22,900 kg and it handled 61,400 passenger movements in 2025, so neither limb applied. Under 10.4.3 its measures did not need to be documented, and the aerodrome was not in breach. It therefore held no plan, no hazard assessment and no dispersal programme, and the three deferrals were made with no hazard assessment before the council. Section 10.4.1 still required reasonable measures, and a plan does not itself fund a fence. That is why this link is the weakest of the contributing links, although on the balance of the evidence it is likely that the threshold left the fence without an owner as a wildlife control and so contributed to its remaining unrepaired.

The timing of the departure then determined whether animals were on the runway. The aerodrome's sighting log for 01/01/2025 to 18/06/2026 held 46 entries, 41 of them kangaroos on or adjacent to the movement area. Of those 41, 38 were timed between one hour before and two hours after last light, and eleven recorded animals on the sealed surface. On 18/06/2026 last light was 17:25, so that window ran from 16:25 to 19:25, and the roll began at 17:30. The pilot in command's account matched the log, since they had seen kangaroos on the strip four or five times, always in the evening and never in daytime. The log records sightings rather than presence, and aerodrome staff go off duty at 18:30, part way through the window, so the pattern may partly reflect when someone was there to see. Even so, the log and the pilot in command's account agree. It is likely that departing within this window contributed to the animals being on the runway.

Why the animals were not found or seen

Operations Manual Part A 8.14.2 states that "At an aerodrome listed in Appendix 8A, the pilot in command shall request a runway inspection from the aerodrome operator prior to the first departure after last light, and shall not commence the take-off roll until the result of that inspection has been passed" (Figure 1). Appendix 8A lists an aerodrome only where a wildlife strike involving a company aircraft has been reported there in the preceding 24 months. Nine aerodromes were listed, Tarlton Springs had never been listed, and the list was last reviewed on 03/03/2025. No provision in Part A asked a crew to report a sighting, and no provision admitted an aerodrome on any other evidence. The criterion could therefore be met only by the kind of occurrence the inspection exists to prevent. The inspection itself would have worked, because the aerodrome reporting officer confirmed that one would have been carried out if asked. The listing criterion very likely contributed by leaving the requirement unarmed at Tarlton Springs.

Because the requirement did not apply, no inspection was requested. The CVR and the CTAF recording held no request for an inspection, no offer of one and no mention of wildlife before departure. The only inspection that day was at 07:35 before the first arrival, with the result "movement area clear". Both crew said they did not consider requesting an inspection, and the pilot in command had expected Tarlton Springs to be on the list and was surprised to find it was not. An inspection would have covered the section between 1,050 m and 1,250 m where the pad and both carcasses were found, and aerodrome staff disperse animals when they find them. An inspection completed some minutes before the roll cannot guarantee a clear runway at the time of departure. It is nevertheless likely that the absence of an inspection contributed to the animals being on the runway at the roll.

The evening service that put SB512 on the runway after last light was approved without the daylight restriction being examined. RRA-041 issue 3 carried the operating restriction "daylight operations only pending review of night lighting and diversion fuel policy". Change record CMR-2025-118, approved by the Head of Flying Operations on 22/05/2025, introduced the first scheduled operation into Tarlton Springs after last light. It assessed the change as "schedule change only", identified no new hazard and answered "No" to route risk assessment review required. RRA-041 was not reopened and no issue 4 exists. The restriction names night lighting and diversion fuel, not wildlife, so a review might have approved the evening service with lighting and fuel conditions and left the departure after last light unchanged. The approver has left the company, and what a review would have concluded cannot be established. However, a review was the only process that would have assessed a night operation at this aerodrome, and SB512 rolled in darkness on its schedule and not because of a delay. It is likely that approving the service without that review contributed to the roll taking place in darkness.

The darkness mattered because it hid the strip beside the seal. The roll began at 17:30, 32 minutes after sunset and 5 minutes after the end of civil twilight, with moonrise not until 22:41 and the moon 14% illuminated. The site visit at the same time of day confirmed that the unlit graded strip either side of the sealed surface cannot be seen from the centreline. The first officer said on the CVR "They came out of the dark on the left of the strip". The first officer saw the animals at around 200 m once they were on the seal, and how long they had been on the strip before that is not known. Animals that reached the seal seconds after entering the strip would have been seen late in daylight as well. The pilot in command was looking at the engine page after V1, as the procedure places them, and said on the CVR "I was heads-in on the engine page after V one". Daylight would still have left the sighting with the first officer, whose attention belongs on the centreline. Two animals crossing the graded strip in daylight would, however, have been visible before they reached the seal. Darkness probably contributed to the late sighting that preceded the reject.

The decision and the stop

The first officer called the animals at 17:30:31 and the pilot in command said "Stopping. I have control." at 17:30:32 (Figure 5). Part B 4.6.4 states "At or above V1 the take-off shall be continued." (Figure 4) The FDR recorded V1 at 112 kt at 17:30:29 and the power levers retarded at 118 kt, 3 seconds and 6 kt past V1. The scheduled accelerate-stop distance was 1,780 m against an ASDA of 1,847 m, a margin of 67 m that assumes the stop begins at or before V1. The reject began 1,152 m along the runway, leaving 695 m of sealed surface. Beginning the stop six knots and three seconds late consumed the margin and more, so it is extremely likely that the reject above V1 contributed to the overrun. A continued take-off would have avoided the overrun, and that is the whole of this judgement.

The pilot in command's air safety report states that they judged continuing would leave the aircraft airborne at night with damage that could not be assessed, over country with no usable option. The pilot in command stated that the decision was not in accordance with the procedure. Neither training nor procedure had prepared the crew for it. The four scripted scenarios in module 4 of the recurrent syllabus were all aircraft system events, namely engine failure at 90 kt, engine fire at 100 kt, a configuration warning at 85 kt, and engine failure at V1 plus 5 kt with the take-off continued. None presented an obstruction or any external hazard on the runway at any speed. No crew had been presented with one in the five training cycles on file, which cover 214 crew in the current cycle alone. Part B 4.6 contained no guidance on an obstruction on the runway at any speed and no amplification of 4.6.4 for a case in which continuing is itself hazardous. Both crew stated independently that every stop or go scenario they had been given was an engine event.

The pilot in command stated that the rule was known and that it was departed from deliberately, so training would not have changed what they knew. On that reading the gap concerns the fleet rather than this reject. However, the decision was made in about a second, with no scenario or guidance against which to make it, and a decision made cold differs from one made against a briefed and practised frame. The reasoning rests on the decision being unrehearsed and not on what guidance would have said. Because that reasoning is balanced against the pilot in command's own account, it is likely that the absence of training and guidance contributed to the take-off being rejected above V1.

Performance assessment PEA-2026-0417 reconstructed a continued take-off from 17:30:32. The aircraft would have reached the animals at the same place within a few hundredths of a second, at about 120 kt and 4 to 5 degrees nose-up, with the main wheels still on the runway and the engines at take-off power. The teardown of the No. 2 propeller found the pitch change actuator cracked through with its oil lost, so the propeller could not have feathered after the impact. Appendix 4C assumes automatic feathering, a retracted gear and an otherwise undamaged aeroplane. In the central case, with the propeller unfeathered, the gear up with its doors open and the right flap damaged, the gross gradient would have been 1.0% against the 2.4% minimum, and the aircraft would have been about 55 ft below the top of the mast 3,400 m beyond the runway end (Figure 6). RRA-041 records no alternate within 200 nm at night, so the aircraft would have had to return to a runway with two carcasses on it. On that reconstruction, rejecting the take-off was probably the safest course of action available.

That conclusion is held at probably and no higher. The damage was done at flight idle and 114 kt, and the teardown could not say whether the pitch change mechanism would have failed in the same way at take-off power. A propeller that feathered would have left about 3.2% gross, and a gradient below the minimum is not itself a crash. Controllability at V2 with the right flap damaged and the right propeller windmilling, and the effect of the propeller's imbalance, were not assessed. The assessment does not lower the reject's contribution to the overrun and does not make the decision compliant with Part B 4.6.4. It also does not show that the pilot in command could have known its result in the second available.

The strike then took the No. 2 propeller out of the stop. Impact at 17:30:33 at 114 kt was one second after the reject began, with both engines already near flight idle. The FDR recorded a lateral acceleration spike of 0.31 g right and a vertical spike of 1.48 g. Three No. 2 propeller blades were damaged beyond limits and animal tissue was recovered from two blade roots, and the breached actuator held the blades near flight idle angle. The No. 2 propeller RPM decayed from the moment of impact and the No. 2 reverse interlock did not make. With the strike this directly recorded, it is virtually certain that the propeller and right main gear struck the two animals. With No. 2 unable to reach ground idle and reverse on No. 1 only, the mean deceleration from maximum braking was 2.6 m/s2, approximately 15% below the value used in the certified data. This shortfall is virtually certain, and it arose directly from the strike. At the certified deceleration from the same point the reconstruction puts the stop at roughly 660 m, inside the 695 m remaining, while at the deceleration achieved it needed 757 m. The overrun was therefore the result of two contributions, the late start of the stop and the strike's effect on deceleration, and neither alone would have carried the aircraft off the end.

The animals' presence on the runway followed directly from the conditions above. Two adult kangaroos were recovered from the runway at 1,188 m and 1,221 m, and the first officer's call at 17:30:31 and the impact at 17:30:33 each confirm it. It is extremely likely that their presence on the sealed surface led to both the reject and the strike.

Unresolved matters

Four northern edge lights above nominal intensity

A photometric check on 25/06/2026, seven days after the occurrence, measured four northern edge lights between the 900 m and 1,200 m markers at 118% to 131% of nominal intensity for stage 3. This was the section the animals crossed, and the remaining lights were within tolerance. The lighting is pilot-activated and runs at one fixed intensity set at the aerodrome's lighting controller, found at stage 3, the setting recorded at commissioning. Crews cannot vary it, and no work on the lighting or its controller was recorded between the occurrence and the check. It is likely that the four lights were at the measured intensity on the night, although nobody measured them at the time.

The matter that could not be settled is whether that intensity delayed detection of the animals and so the reject. The pilot in command recalled the lighting as brighter than wanted, a corridor of light with everything outside it dark, and said that with pilot-activated lighting there was nobody to ask to turn it down. Brighter lights would deepen the contrast between that corridor and the dark strip beside it, from which the animals came. However, the first officer, who actually saw the animals, described the lighting as normal and saw them completely clearly once they were on the seal. The first officer also said that with only two daylight landings to compare against they were not well placed to judge whether it was unusual. Darkness alone explains why nothing off the seal was seen, and the pilot in command's non-detection is explained by attention on the engine page after V1. [NOT ESTABLISHED: any evidence relating edge light intensity to detection of an animal on or beside the runway]. Whether the intensity delayed detection is about as likely as not, and the matter remains unresolved. Nothing from it is carried into the findings.

Flight crew fatigue

The take-off was 11 hours into a duty that began at a 06:30 sign-on and had been extended that morning from three sectors to five, when the crew took the evening rotation from a crew member who reported unfit. Both crew described themselves in interview as tired at that point, and the pilot in command said that if asked to fly another sector they would have declined. Against that, both described the tiredness as ordinary and not impairing. The pilot in command said they were not struggling and the first officer said it was a normal five-sector day with a proper break in Port Carrick. The duty was planned at 13 hours against a 13 hour 30 minute maximum, and the pilot in command's duty and rest in the preceding 7 days were within limits with no variations. The recorded performance showed none of the usual signs, with power levers at idle in 0.6 seconds, maximum braking in 2 seconds at the fast end of the fleet distribution, callouts made on time, and no error of omission on the roll.

Being tired after 11 hours is not the same as being fatigued to a degree that degrades performance, and no available evidence reaches that distinction. Settling it would require a detailed fatigue assessment of sleep history and the duty pattern before 18/06/2026. Whether the crew were fatigued is about as likely as not, and the matter remains unresolved. Even had fatigue been present, every mechanism it would have worked through on the roll is contradicted by the recorded data. The one decision it could plausibly have touched, not requesting an inspection, was never prompted by any document. Nothing from this matter is carried into the findings.

Factors that increased risk without influencing this occurrence

The evening rotation was rostered as the fourth and fifth sectors of a duty planned at between 12 hours 45 minutes and 13 hours 15 minutes against a 13 hour 30 minute maximum, on each of the 289 days it operated between 14/07/2025 and 18/06/2026. On six of those days, including 18/06/2026, a rostered crew member reported unfit and the rotation went to a crew already on duty, extending that crew's day from three sectors to five. It is unlikely that this contributed to the occurrence, because the recorded response times were at the fast end of the fleet distribution and the decision that a long duty might have affected, whether to request an inspection, was not prompted by any document. The pattern nonetheless puts the last sector of the longest duty into an aerodrome with no alternate within 200 nm at night and limited engineering support. It is likely that this standing exposure increased risk, because it is present on every operation of the rotation and was not removed by its failure to bite on this occasion.

The floor proximity escape path lighting on this type is checked only by a dedicated functional test at the maintenance programme's 24-month interval, and the pre-flight test illuminates only the ceiling emergency lights and exit signs. On VH-SBQ, a functional check on 24/06/2026 found two of the six floor segments aft of row 16 on the left side dark on battery power, traced to a failed common ballast. The first officer's observation of unlit sections of the aisle floor strip during the disembarkation prompted the check. The last functional test had been 11 months before the occurrence and inside the interval, so no check available to the crew or a line engineer could have found the defect. It is unlikely that this influenced the occurrence, because no evacuation was commanded, the main cabin lights were on, and the disembarkation by the forward airstair took 4 minutes 8 seconds without urgency. In a different occurrence involving fire, smoke or a night evacuation, two dark segments in the aft cabin could be the difference between an orderly exit and a blocked one. This monitoring gap very likely increased risk, and the matter is still being examined. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the same ballast part is fitted across the fleet].

Considered and not found contributing

A tailwind was considered because a stop that runs 62 m past the end invites a question about the wind. The automatic weather station's observations gave a headwind component of 5 to 7 kt on runway 09, and the FDR gave a headwind component of 4 to 6 kt throughout, with no tailwind at any point. A tailwind component during the roll and the stop was very unlikely.

A No. 2 engine power loss before the reject was considered because a reject at 118 kt is most commonly an engine event. Both engines were within 0.1% torque of each other from power set until the power levers were retarded at 17:30:32, with fuel flow, ITT and propeller RPM within normal scatter and no caution, warning or exceedance recorded. The CVR contains no engine-related call, and the borescope of both engines found no pre-existing damage. The No. 2 propeller damage and RPM decay began at 17:30:33, after the reject, so the loss followed the strike. A No. 2 engine power loss before the reject was very unlikely.

Findings

From the evidence available, the following findings are made with respect to the rejected take-off and runway overrun at Tarlton Springs. These findings should not be read as apportioning blame or liability to any particular organisation or individual.

The investigation applied a standard of proof of "Likely or probable": a proposition is established at a probability of 65% or more and not established at 35% or less, and anything between is inconclusive.

Contributing factors

  • The northern perimeter fence between the 700 m and 1,300 m runway markers was recorded as failed in 04/2023, with animals observed passing through, and was deferred unfunded at three successive budget rounds. This existed with virtual certainty. It probably contributed to the occurrence because the failed section was the route by which the animals most likely reached the movement area, although it was not established that a replacement fence would have excluded kangaroos.
  • Tarlton Springs held no documented wildlife hazard management plan because the threshold in AS-139 10.4.2 did not apply to it, and the aerodrome was not in breach. This existed with virtual certainty. It probably contributed to the occurrence because no hazard assessment or owner was in place when the fence repair was deferred, although a plan would not of itself have funded the fence. (Safety Issue)
  • The evening service was approved through CMR-2025-118 as a schedule change only, without reopening RRA-041 issue 3, which restricted Tarlton Springs to daylight operations. This existed with virtual certainty. It probably contributed to the occurrence because a review would have had to assess a night operation at the aerodrome, although what a review would have concluded cannot be known because the approver has left the company. (Safety Issue)
  • Appendix 8A of the operator's Operations Manual Part A listed an aerodrome only where a wildlife strike involving a company aircraft had been reported there in the preceding 24 months, so Tarlton Springs could not be listed and the Part A 8.14.2 runway inspection requirement did not apply to it. This existed with virtual certainty. It very probably contributed to the occurrence because the control could be triggered only by the outcome it exists to prevent. (Safety Issue)
  • No runway inspection was requested before the departure after last light. This existed with virtual certainty. It probably contributed to the occurrence because an inspection would have covered the section of runway where both carcasses were found and the aerodrome reporting officer confirmed one would have been carried out if asked, although an inspection some minutes before the roll could not guarantee the runway remained clear.
  • Neither the operator's training syllabus nor Part B 4.6 covered an obstruction on the runway during the take-off roll. This very probably existed. It probably contributed to the occurrence because the decision at and after V1 was made without a practised or briefed basis, although the pilot in command stated they knew the continue-at-V1 rule and departed from it deliberately. (Safety Issue)
  • The take-off roll began at 17:30, 5 minutes after the end of civil twilight, with no moon and no natural light on the strip. This existed with virtual certainty. It probably contributed to the occurrence because the strip either side of the sealed surface could not be seen from the centreline, although the time the animals had been on the strip before reaching the seal is not known.
  • The departure fell within the period from one hour before to two hours after last light, in which 38 of the 41 kangaroo entries in the aerodrome's sighting log were timed. This very probably existed. It probably contributed to the occurrence, although the log records sightings rather than presence and aerodrome staff go off duty at 18:30, so the pattern may partly reflect when someone was there to see.
  • Two kangaroos crossed the strip onto the sealed runway and were on the surface at 1,188 m and 1,221 m. This existed with virtual certainty. It very probably contributed to the occurrence because both the reject and the strike followed directly from the animals being on the surface.
  • The take-off was rejected at 118 kt, 6 kt and 3 seconds after V1, with 695 m of sealed surface remaining against a scheduled accelerate-stop margin of 67 m. This existed with virtual certainty. It very probably contributed to the overrun because a stop begun at that point consumed the margin, and a continued take-off would have avoided the overrun. The reconstruction of a continued take-off indicated that rejecting was probably the safest course available, so this finding does not show the decision was unreasonable. That assessment does not alter the reject's contribution to the overrun, does not make the decision compliant with Part B 4.6.4, and does not show that the pilot in command could have known it in the second available.
  • The aircraft's No. 2 propeller and right main gear struck the two kangaroos at 114 kt. This existed with virtual certainty. It contributed to the occurrence with virtual certainty because the strike destroyed the No. 2 propeller's ability to reach ground idle or reverse.
  • The deceleration achieved during the stop was about 15% below the certified accelerate-stop value, at 2.6 m/s2. This existed with virtual certainty. It contributed to the overrun with virtual certainty because the reconstruction put the stop at roughly 660 m at the certified deceleration, inside the 695 m remaining, against 757 m at the deceleration achieved.

Other factors that increased risk

  • The evening Tarlton Springs rotation was rostered on 289 days as the fourth and fifth sectors of a duty planned at 12 hours 45 minutes to 13 hours 15 minutes, against a maximum of 13 hours 30 minutes, and six times was reassigned to a crew already on duty. This existed with virtual certainty. It unlikely influenced this occurrence because the recorded crew response was at the fast end of the fleet distribution and no error of omission was recorded on the roll. It probably increased risk because the pattern is a standing exposure at an aerodrome with no alternate within 200 nm at night. (Safety Issue)
  • The floor proximity escape path lighting on this aircraft type is checked only by a functional test at a 24-month interval and is not covered by the pre-flight test. This existed with virtual certainty, and on VH-SBQ the gap held a defect with two of six segments dark on the left side aft of row 16. It unlikely influenced this occurrence because no evacuation was commanded and the cabin lights were on throughout. It very probably increased risk because the state of the escape path lighting between functional tests is unknown. (Safety Issue)

Other findings

  • Maximum braking was established 2 seconds after the reject decision, against a fleet mean of 3.2 seconds. It very probably decreased risk because the aircraft stopped 62 m into the 90 m runway end safety area at low speed, upright and on the extended centreline, and a stop begun at the fleet mean would have carried the aircraft an estimated further 30 to 40 m.
  • A tailwind component during the take-off roll and stop was very unlikely to have existed, because the aerodrome observations and the recorded aircraft data both gave a headwind component throughout.
  • A No. 2 engine power loss before the reject decision was very unlikely to have existed, because both engines were within 0.1% torque of each other until the power levers were retarded and the No. 2 propeller damage began after the reject, at impact.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any finding on regulatory oversight, as no material on it is held]

Safety issues and actions

This section sets out each safety issue the investigation identified, with the safety action taken or proposed against it, followed by the immediate actions after the occurrence.

Evening service approved without reopening the daylight-only route risk assessment

The operator approved a scheduled evening rotation to Tarlton Springs through change record CMR-2025-118 as a schedule change only and did not reopen RRA-041, which restricted the aerodrome to daylight operations. On the evidence, the approval was likely a condition that put SB512 on the runway after last light.

The Head of Flying Operations suspended the evening Tarlton Springs service after the occurrence, and the suspension was in place from 19/06/2026.

Appendix 8A listing criterion

Appendix 8A of the operator's Operations Manual Part A lists an aerodrome only where a company wildlife strike has been reported there in the preceding 24 months. Because the runway inspection requirement in 8.14.2 applies only at listed aerodromes, it could not apply at Tarlton Springs before a strike had occurred there (Figure 1). It is very likely that the requirement, had it applied, would have led to an inspection request before the departure.

The Head of Flying Operations amended Appendix 8A by temporary revision TR-2026-04 on 26/06/2026 to list Tarlton Springs. The 8.14.2 inspection requirement therefore applies to every departure there after last light pending the permanent change. This action is closed.

The investigation proposes the following safety action, which was open on 02/07/2026 with a response due by 30/09/2026.

  • That the operator replace the Appendix 8A listing criterion so that an aerodrome is listed on wildlife exposure rather than on a reported strike, and add a route risk assessment trigger for any aerodrome first operated into after last light. The present criterion can only be met by the occurrence the control exists to prevent, so no aerodrome can be listed before a strike has happened there.

No training or guidance for an obstruction during the take-off roll

Neither the operator's rejected take-off guidance in Part B 4.6 nor its recurrent simulator syllabus addressed an obstruction on the runway at or after V1 (Figure 4). It is probable that this left the pilot in command making the reject decision without a briefed or practised basis for it.

The investigation proposes the following safety action, which was open on 02/07/2026 with a response due by 30/09/2026.

  • That the operator, with the type certificate holder, develop guidance and simulator training for an obstruction on the runway during the take-off roll, including at and after V1. The guidance should state that the continue-at-V1 rule rests on take-off data for an engine failure on an otherwise undamaged aeroplane, and should give crews a basis for the decision when an obstruction ahead means neither the stop nor the go is the one the data describe.

Failed northern perimeter fence

The northern boundary fence between the 700 m and 1,300 m runway markers had been recorded as failed since 04/2023 and was deferred unfunded at three budget rounds (Figure 2). It is probable that this section was the route by which the two kangaroos reached the runway.

The aerodrome operator funded works register item WR-221 from the 2026 contingency and programmed the 140 m replacement of the northern boundary fence for 09/2026. A temporary electric wire was installed on 25/06/2026. This proactive action is in progress.

AS-139 threshold and the absence of a documented wildlife plan

Aerodrome Standard AS-139 10.4.2 requires a documented wildlife hazard management plan only above 27,000 kg maximum take-off weight or 350,000 passenger movements a year. Tarlton Springs fell below both limbs and held no plan, although it was not in breach of the standard. It is probable that the absence of a plan left the failed fence to be treated as a deferrable maintenance item.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any safety action or recommendation on the AS-139 threshold or on documented wildlife measures at aerodromes below it]

Rostering of the evening rotation

The evening rotation was rostered on all 289 days of operation as the fourth and fifth sectors of a duty planned to finish within 45 minutes of the 13 hour 30 minute maximum. On six of those days, including 18/06/2026, it was reassigned to a crew already on duty. The roster was unlikely to have influenced this occurrence, but it is likely that this standing exposure increases risk on every operation of the rotation.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any safety action recorded against the roster]

Floor escape path lighting monitoring

The pre-flight emergency lighting test on this type does not illuminate or monitor the floor proximity escape path segments, whose only check is a functional test at a 24-month interval. On VH-SBQ, two of the six segments on the left side aft of row 16 were dark with a failed common ballast. The monitoring gap was unlikely to have influenced this occurrence because the disembarkation was conducted without urgency with the main cabin lights on. It is very likely that the gap increases risk, because the state of this defence on any aircraft of the type is unknown between functional tests.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any safety action recorded against the 24-month functional test interval or the pre-flight test coverage]

Immediate actions after the occurrence

The aerodrome operator closed the aerodrome pending inspection and the removal of animal remains and propeller debris. The aircraft was quarantined at Tarlton Springs, and the operator's engineering representative removed the FDR and CVR on 18/06/2026 and couriered them to the operator's flight data section. Both flight crew were stood down from duty and tested for drugs and alcohol, and both results were negative.

The aerodrome kept a paper sighting log of 46 wildlife entries from 01/2025 to 06/2026, and no airline had asked for it.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any action to make the aerodrome sighting log available to operators]

The supporting extract attached to it is the wildlife sighting log, not the inspection log. - Floor escape path lighting checked only every 24 months, not pre-flight: the factor is marked as not finalised, pending the engineering answer on ballast commonality across the fleet. The draft does not use the 200 m figure. - No runway inspection requested before departing after last light: the influence note refers to a "fence pad" found in the 1,050 m to 1,250 m section.
